summary: Analyzes how different link-state IGP implementations, and especially their Shortest Path First (SPF) delay algorithms and trigger strategies, affect micro-loops. A micro-loop is a brief packet-forwarding loop that can occur while routers update their paths at different times. It is informational.

eli5.summary: When a road closes, drivers may get new directions at different times and briefly go in circles. This document studies how the waiting time before recalculating directions affects those short-lived circles.

questions: how spf timers affect routing loops
how does spf delay affect routing micro-loops
why do routers converge at different times
what is the impact of mixing routing implementations
subtitle: How router coordination timing shapes packet-forwarding loops

tldr.problem: When a network link fails, routers update their routes at different times, and this asynchronous convergence can briefly create micro-loops where packets loop between routers. Different implementations use different SPF (Shortest Path First) delays to batch topology changes.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC analyzes how SPF delay algorithms and trigger strategies affect the likelihood and duration of micro-loops when implementations with different timing strategies are mixed in one network.
tldr.outcome: Using consistent SPF delay algorithms across all routers reduces the probability and duration of micro-loops, encouraging standardization of SPF behavior in link-state IGP protocols.

today: RFC 8541 is Informational and has not been obsoleted. It provides analysis of the micro-loop problem and has motivated follow-up work in standardizing SPF delay algorithms, notably RFC 8405.

sections.title: Micro-loops in Link-State Routing
sections.content:
Micro-loops are brief packet-forwarding loops that occur when two or more routers in a hop-by-hop forwarding network update their forwarding tables at different times. Link-state IGP protocols like OSPF and IS-IS run the Shortest Path First algorithm to compute consistent, loop-free paths from a shared topology database. However, when a network event (such as a link failure) occurs, routers do not all recompute and update their forwarding information base (FIB) simultaneously. This asynchronous convergence creates a window where some routers have updated their routes and others have not, leading to transient loops.

The RFC focuses on the role of SPF delay timers in creating or preventing micro-loops, and on the impact of mixing different SPF implementations in multi-vendor networks.
sections.eli5: Imagine drivers updating their GPS directions at different speeds. Before everyone knows about a new route, some drivers might send others on circles.

sections.title: How SPF Delays Cause Micro-loops
sections.content:
A micro-loop is most likely to occur when two routers do not update their paths for the same destination at nearly the same time. Several factors affect the probability and duration of micro-loops: the delay in notification of a failure, the SPF delay (the wait before computing new routes), the SPF computation time itself, the order in which SPF is computed for different areas or topologies, and the speed at which forwarding tables are updated.

The SPF delay plays a critical role, especially during periods of network churn (many rapid changes). When routers use different SPF delay values, the time gap between their convergence increases, which increases the window for micro-loops to occur. The RFC illustrates this with a network topology where router S reaches a prefix Px via D, but can reroute through E when the S-D link fails. If S converges faster than E (due to SPF delays or other factors), S will forward packets to E, but E has not yet learned the failure and forwards them back to S, creating a loop.
sections.eli5: If one router learns about a link failure quickly but another learns slowly, the fast one might send packets to the slow one, which doesn't know yet and sends them back.

sections.title: SPF Delay Algorithms
sections.content:
Implementations use two main strategies to delay SPF computation, attempting to batch multiple topology changes into a single computation and reduce CPU load.

Two-Step Delay uses four parameters: a rapid delay (e.g., 50 ms), a count of rapid runs allowed (e.g., 3), a slow delay (e.g., 1 s), and a wait time before returning to rapid delay (e.g., 2 s). When events arrive frequently, the algorithm moves to the slow delay after exhausting its rapid runs. Exponential Back-Off Delay alternates between fast mode (first delay, e.g., 50 ms) and back-off mode (delay increases exponentially from an initial increment, e.g., 50 ms, up to a maximum, e.g., 1 s). Both strategies allow the router to revert to fast mode after a quiet period (wait time).

These are not standardized in most protocol specifications, so different vendors implement them differently or not at all.
sections.eli5: Some routers wait a little before recalculating (fast), then wait longer if changes keep happening (slow). Others speed up first, then slow down exponentially. No rule requires them to do the same.

sections.title: Mixing Strategies in Multi-Vendor Networks
sections.content:
When one router uses two-step delay and another uses exponential back-off, especially with different parameter values, their SPF computations become misaligned. The RFC demonstrates this with detailed timing tables showing a sequence of prefix state changes followed by a link failure. When S (using two-step delay with rapid delay = 150 ms) and E (using exponential back-off with first delay = 150 ms) receive the same events, the exponential algorithm moves to higher delays faster, causing S to converge ahead of E. This creates a 450 ms window of micro-loops (from 1162 ms to 1626 ms) in one scenario, and a 154 ms window in another.

Even with a single type of event, misaligned delays produce micro-loops. The issue is compounded by other implementation differences in SPF computation order, reachability computation, and FIB update speed.
sections.eli5: If one router waits 150ms then 300ms then 1s, and another waits 150ms then 300ms then 600ms, they get out of sync and packets bounce between them.

sections.title: Benefits of Standardized Behavior
sections.content: When both routers use the same SPF delay algorithm with the same parameters, they converge more nearly simultaneously, reducing the probability and duration of micro-loops. Using the same timing sequence as the mixed-strategy example above, but with both S and E employing an identical SPF delay, the micro-loop window shrinks from 450 ms to just 17 ms (from 1162 ms to 1177 ms). The RFC notes that micro-loops can still occur due to other factors like router computation speed and FIB update time, but standardizing SPF delay behavior is a practical step that service providers can take to reduce the problem. RFC 8405 defines one such standardized SPF delay algorithm for link-state IGPs.
sections.eli5: If both routers wait the same way, they learn about failures at nearly the same time, and packets barely loop at all.
